scene.testo: They handed him one chart. It showed his U-boats vanishing, month after month. Then the Allied officers asked Admiral Karl Dönitz a single question. Why did your submarine war fail? His answer named one invention.
He did not blame his crews. He did not blame his shipyards. He did not blame Hitler. He pointed to one Allied development, and he ranked its importance beside the atomic bomb. Hold that thought.

Nobody alive knew that battle better than he did. He had commanded it from the first torpedo to the last. Yet on the day his campaign collapsed, the thing that exposed his boats was sitting where he never thought to look.
To understand his answer, you must see how close he came to winning. In 1942, his U-boats sank more ships than in any other year of the war. Many of those ships went down just off American shores.

German codebreakers were reading some Allied convoy codes. So his boats often knew where to wait. Dönitz ran the whole battle by radio from headquarters, moving his wolf packs across the ocean like pieces on a map.

At the height of that success, he later admitted, one worry nagged at him. Air power might someday force his boats beneath the waves. Few people around him wanted to hear it. Then came the spring of 1943.

This was the chart in the courtroom. Month after month, the lines fell. The numbers measured Allied ships lost and German boats destroyed. By his own account, the Atlantic had turned against him within weeks.

Before that spring, Germany lost roughly one U-boat for every 100,000 tons of Allied shipping sunk. In May 1943, the ratio collapsed to one boat for every 10,000 tons. The exchange rate had fallen tenfold.
His own war diary called the losses in May unbearable. So the question was simple. What changed? At Nuremberg, Dönitz answered without hesitation. And the answer came from the sky, not the sea.

He said aircraft, with the surprise they allowed and the radar they now carried, had broken the U-boat war. A submarine was fast and dangerous only on the surface. Now it could be found there, day or night.

Detection came from beyond the horizon. Allied sets could spot a surfaced boat from many miles away, in darkness or fog. German warning receivers could not hear the new signals. The old defenses had gone silent.

Then came the reach of the aircraft. American Liberators, built for long range, flew far out over the Atlantic. They covered the middle of the ocean, where land-based planes had never been able to go before.

Small American escort carriers sailed with the convoys as well. Each carried its own squadron of Avenger torpedo bombers. A U-boat crew on the surface often did not know it had been found until aircraft were overhead.

By Dönitz's own count, that month, aircraft probably destroyed about twenty of his boats. Ships accounted for only eight. Every number pointed upward, to the sky. His staff took that as the full explanation.

But on May 19, his war diary recorded something radar alone could not explain. His staff read an intercepted British situation report. It placed twenty-five German submarines in one stretch of the North Atlantic.

It was exactly where his two patrol lines were waiting. Every position was correct. Twenty-five boats, spread across hundreds of miles of ocean, all marked accurately at the same moment. How was that possible?
The entry in his war diary is a single line. The position of the aircraft, it suggested, might be the only source. Dönitz found the explanation he wanted. He kept looking up at the sky.
That same day, near the same convoy, his younger son Peter was lost with his boat. Peter served as a watch officer on U-954. The admiral who ordered the battle had just lost a child in it.

Five days later, Dönitz gave way. On May 24, he ordered his boats out of the North Atlantic, toward waters with fewer aircraft. In a message to every commander, he blamed enemy location devices and surprise air attacks.
Then he added a second instruction. His headquarters must keep up heavy radio traffic, so the enemy would not see how few boats were left. He wanted to deceive the Allies with his own radio.

His operators typed the order letter by letter, as they sent everything else. They used a machine Dönitz believed no one could break. He had checked it more than once. His intelligence chief told him the enemy could not read it.

It was called Enigma. British codebreakers at Bletchley Park had been reading U-boat traffic again since December 1942. In May 1943, the United States Navy began testing its own codebreaking machines in Dayton, Ohio.

By the end of that year, American machines were doing most of the work. A wartime American study of the battle put it plainly. In the German command, codebreaking was never seriously suspected. And so the Americans began to use it.

In June 1943, the escort carrier USS Bogue sailed to a spot where German submarines waited to refuel. Ultra, the code name for intelligence from intercepted German signals, had located them. Her Avengers found the boats.

On that cruise, Bogue's planes sank two German submarines, one of them a tanker meant to refuel the others. A later American report called it the first U-boat sinking in a purely offensive operation by the United States.

Another escort carrier, USS Card, under Captain Arnold Isbell, sank eleven German submarines before the war ended. Hunter groups like these did not wait for convoys to be attacked. They went looking for the boats themselves.

Yet Dönitz was not simply wrong. Codebreaking alone cannot sink a submarine. That same American study noted that improved Allied radar, which Dönitz knew about, had played a decisive part. The two worked together.

Most historians today credit several factors working together. Longer-range aircraft. Better radar. Hunter groups that attacked, not waited. And broken codes that guided them. Radar found the boats. Enigma told the Allies where to point it.

After the surrender, before the Nuremberg trial, the Allies had asked Dönitz to write down why he lost. The American Office of Naval Intelligence later published his essay. British officers questioned him as well.

At first he delivered an angry speech about being treated as a war criminal. Then, according to their report, he calmed down, turned friendly, and asked what they wanted to know. This time, he gave a second reason.
He said Allied bombing had delayed his new generation of U-boats. They would have been ready by the autumn of 1944. In that sense, he told them, the air offensive had decided the war for the Allies.

The court sentenced him to ten years in prison. In 1958, he published his memoirs. He wrote that his codes had been tested again and again, and found unbreakable. Even then, he said, he could not be certain.

The world learned the truth in 1974, when the Ultra secret was finally revealed. Dönitz was still alive, aged eighty-two. On the day he lost his patrol lines, his son, and the Atlantic, he had blamed the sky.

He never suspected the machine on his own desk. He was not the only one the Allies questioned. When they asked Hitler's armaments minister, Albert Speer, which raid hurt Germany most, he named not a city, but one day.
To hear more of what the men on the other side said in their own words, subscribe and watch Speer's story next. It is on your screen now.

descrizione:
In 1946, the Allies asked Admiral Karl Dönitz, who commanded Germany's U-boat fleet, why the submarine war was lost. His answer pointed to Allied radar and air power. But the war diary, the Enigma machine, and the codebreakers at Bletchley Park tell a deeper story.

This documentary follows the Battle of the Atlantic in 1943, the collapse of the wolf packs in May, the loss of Dönitz's son Peter, and the secret of Ultra that stayed hidden until 1974. It draws on interrogation reports, Nuremberg testimony, and Dönitz's own memoirs.

Watch to the end to see what Albert Speer named as the most damaging day. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more history told through the words of those who were there.
